text.content: Not every multi-agent system needs a hierarchy. For most of what Sofia is building at Cascadia — an Intake Agent routing to a handful of specialists — a single coordinator managing the specialists directly is exactly right. Adding another management layer above that would just be extra machinery without any real coordination problem to solve.

text.content: Hierarchical orchestration becomes valuable when the problem grows large enough that a single coordinator cannot reasonably manage every specialist — dozens of them, spread across different domains — without the coordination itself becoming a bottleneck. This lesson is about recognising when a hierarchy is solving a real coordination problem rather than just adding structure for its own sake.

text.content: What is hierarchical orchestration?

rich_text.plain_text: What is hierarchical orchestration?

text.content: In hierarchical orchestration, agents are organized into levels.

rich_text.plain_text: In hierarchical orchestration, agents are organized into levels.

text.content: A top-level agent acts as a manager. Rather than performing work directly, it decides which lower-level agents should handle different parts of the problem. Those agents may then coordinate their own specialist agents before returning results upward.

text.content: Why not always use a hierarchy?

rich_text.plain_text: Why not always use a hierarchy?

text.content: A hierarchy introduces additional coordination.

rich_text.plain_text: A hierarchy introduces additional coordination.

text.content: Each additional layer introduces extra coordination overhead. More agents means more prompts to maintain, more messages being passed between components, and more opportunities for misunderstandings or failures. Troubleshooting also becomes more difficult because issues can originate at multiple levels of the hierarchy rather than in a single workflow. As a result, hierarchical orchestration should only be introduced when the benefits of distributing responsibility outweigh the additional complexity.

text.content: Scenario 1: Large IT support organizations

rich_text.plain_text: Scenario 1: Large IT support organizations

text.content: Consider a global IT support organization that receives thousands of requests every day. Some requests involve simple password resets, while others relate to billing questions, network outages, security incidents, or infrastructure problems. As the number and variety of requests grow, it becomes increasingly difficult for a single coordinator to manage every specialist directly. A hierarchical structure allows responsibility to be divided across teams, making the system easier to scale and manage.

text.content: Rather than sending every request directly to individual specialists, the top-level manager first decides which team should handle the issue. Requests related to infrastructure are passed to an Infrastructure Team Lead, security-related issues are delegated to a Security Team Lead, and customer-facing problems are directed to a Customer Support Team Lead. Each team lead then coordinates the specialists within their own area of responsibility.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: Hierarchical orchestration is the most structured coordination pattern in the multi-agent toolkit. It becomes worthwhile only when the number of specialists or the diversity of domains makes a single coordinator impractical. Small workflows are better served by sequential, parallel, or single-level routing patterns.
